title: He Grew Up Playing Tape-Ball Cricket in Peshawar. On Sunday, Rahmat Shah Became Afghanistan's First 1,000-Run Test Batter.
excerpt: The 32-year-old reached the milestone against India in Mullanpur, a career built in refugee tournaments and borrowed grounds, now etched permanently in Test cricket's record books.
body:
Afghanistan's Rahmat Shah became the first player from his country to score 1,000 runs in Test cricket on Sunday, reaching the milestone during the second day of the one-off Test against India at the Maharaja Yadavindra Singh International Cricket Stadium in New Chandigarh.

The landmark arrived with an edge off Indian debutant Manav Suthar that raced to the fine-leg boundary. Shah, 32, had attempted to drive through the covers but the ball took a thick inside edge, narrowly missed leg stump, and ran away for four. There was no fielder stationed at fine leg. It was an unorthodox boundary to mark an extraordinary achievement — a career built not on privilege or infrastructure, but on stubborn persistence.

## From Refugee Camp to Record Books

Shah was born in Peshawar, Pakistan, in 1993, into a family that had fled Afghanistan during the civil war. He grew up playing street cricket with tape-ball setups, far from the manicured academies that produce most Test cricketers. His path to the Afghan national team ran through refugee tournaments and age-group selection camps in Kabul, a city that was still rebuilding when he first picked up a proper cricket bat.

Afghanistan played their inaugural Test match against India in Bengaluru in 2018. Shah, batting at number three, scored 5 and 0 in a heavy defeat. But it was a beginning. He followed that up with 98 against Ireland in 2019 — dismissed two runs short of what would have been Afghanistan's first Test century, chopping on to the stumps off Tim Murtagh.

That heartbreak fuelled what came next. Later that year, against Bangladesh in Chattogram, Shah scored 102 to become the first Afghan to make a Test century. He celebrated it with his father's name on his chest, a tradition he has maintained ever since.

## The Numbers Tell a Story of Grit

Afghanistan have played just nine Tests since their Full Member status was confirmed in 2017. They have won two, lost five, and drawn two. They do not have a home ground — their "home" Tests have been held in Dehradun, Greater Noida, Abu Dhabi, and Lucknow. They do not have a domestic first-class system that produces battle-hardened red-ball batters.

In that context, Shah's career reads differently. His 1,000 runs have come in 16 innings across nine matches. He averages above 40 — a number that would be respectable for any Test batter, but is remarkable for one who gets to play five-day cricket perhaps twice a year. His 231 not out against Zimbabwe in Bulawayo in 2024 remains the highest individual score by an Afghan in Tests.

## What It Means for Afghan Cricket's Diaspora

For the roughly six million Afghans scattered across the globe — in Fremont, California, in Southall, London, in Peshawar, Pakistan — Shah's achievement carries weight beyond a statistical milestone. Cricket has been the one constant that connects a fractured diaspora. The Afghan Premier League, broadcast on social media, draws viewers from refugee camps in Pakistan and living rooms in Toronto alike.

Shah himself embodies this connection. He speaks Pashto at home, trained in Pakistan's club cricket system, and has spent his professional career representing a country many of his teammates have never lived in full-time. His 1,000 runs are not just a personal benchmark. They are evidence that Afghan cricket, still in its adolescence, is producing batters with the temperament and technique to survive against the best.

## The Match Situation

India declared at 564 for 8, built on centuries from captain Shubman Gill (126) and KL Rahul (100), along with Rishabh Pant's breezy 81 and Washington Sundar's composed 52 not out. Mohammad Saleem Safi's six-wicket haul was Afghanistan's primary bright spot with the ball.

In response, Afghanistan found themselves at 113 for 5 at stumps, trailing by 451 runs. Suthar, the Indian debutant, claimed three wickets for 21 runs in his first 16 overs, bowling with a control that belied his inexperience. Prasidh Krishna chipped in with two wickets.

Shah, unbeaten on 43, was the only Afghan batter to find any sustained rhythm. He faces a near-impossible task on Day 3: avoid the follow-on, extend the match, and in doing so, add a few more runs to a record that already belongs to him alone.
